woof = pl.read_parquet(ub + "data/imagewoof_1000.parquet")

The embeddings we need are stored inside the Parquet file, but the picture grids
still need the image files themselves on disk. This cell downloads them the first
time you run it and does nothing on later runs (or if you already have them).

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
import os
import urllib.request

for row in woof.iter_rows(named=True):
    if not os.path.exists(row["filepath"]):
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(row["filepath"]), exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(ub + row["filepath"], row["filepath"])
```

### Questions

`woof` holds 1,000 photographs of dogs from ten breeds. Each row is one photograph:
`filepath` points to the image file and `label` gives the breed. The columns `vit`
and `siglip` hold precomputed embeddings of each image, as in the chapter.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save
it to a variable.

1. Count the number of photographs of each breed (`label`).

```{python}
(
    woof
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.label)
)
```

2. Show one photograph of each breed, as in the chapter, with
`DSImage.plot_image_grid(woof.group_by(c.label).first(), ncol=5)`. Which breeds do
you think will be hard to tell apart?

```{python}
DSImage.plot_image_grid(woof.group_by(c.label).first(), ncol=5)
```

The beagle and the English foxhound are both tricolor hounds and look very similar.
The Australian terrier, border terrier, and Shih Tzu are all small, shaggy dogs. The
Samoyed and the Old English sheepdog are much easier to recognize.

3. Select the columns `filepath`, `label`, and `vit` and keep the first three rows.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .select(c.filepath, c.label, c.vit)
    .head(3)
)
```

Each `vit` value is a list of 768 numbers. No single number has a meaning of its
own; what matters is which images have embeddings close to each other.

4. Project the `vit` embeddings into two dimensions. Pipe `woof` into `umap` with
`features=[c.vit]` and `random_state=42`, and then call `.predict(full=True)`.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .pipe(
        umap,
        features=[c.vit],
        random_state=42
    )
    .predict(full=True)
)
```

5. Take the code from the previous question and draw a scatter plot with `dr0` on the
x-axis and `dr1` on the y-axis, colored by `label`.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .pipe(
        umap,
        features=[c.vit],
        random_state=42
    )
    .predict(full=True)
    .ggplot(aes(c.dr0, c.dr1))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.label))
)
```

Most breeds form their own tight, separate cluster. The exception is the beagle and
the English foxhound, which share one cluster at the bottom left.

6. The block below is given. It loads the SigLIP model and builds a text embedding of
the phrase "a photo of a ..." for each of the ten breeds. The result is saved as
`breed_embed`, with one row per breed. Run it and look at the table.

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
siglip = SigLIPEmbedder()

breed_embed = (
    woof
    .select(text = c.label.unique())
    .sort(c.text)
    .with_columns(
        prompt = pl.lit("a photo of a ") + c.text.str.replace_all("_", " ")
    )
    .with_columns(
        siglip_txt = c.prompt.map_elements(
            siglip.embed_text, return_dtype=pl.List(pl.Float32)
        )
    )
)
breed_embed
```

7. Filter `breed_embed` to the row where `text` is `"golden_retriever"`, and
cross-join `woof` to it with `.join(..., how="cross")`. Add a column
`sim_score = dot_product(c.siglip, c.siglip_txt)`, sort from the highest to the
lowest score, keep the first 8 rows, and show them with `DSImage.plot_image_grid`
labeled by `label`.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .join(breed_embed.filter(c.text == "golden_retriever"), how="cross")
    .with_columns(
        sim_score = dot_product(c.siglip, c.siglip_txt)
    )
    .sort(c.sim_score, descending=True)
    .head(8)
    .pipe(DSImage.plot_image_grid, label_name="label", ncol=4)
)
```

All eight photographs are golden retrievers. The model was never given any of our
labels; it learned from images and captions that this look goes with those words.

8. Now classify every photograph. Cross-join `woof` to all of `breed_embed`, compute
`sim_score` as before, and sort from highest to lowest. Keep the best breed for each
photograph with `.group_by(c.filepath).head(1)`, and compute the share of photographs
where the true `label` matches the predicted breed `text`.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .join(breed_embed, how="cross")
    .with_columns(
        sim_score = dot_product(c.siglip, c.siglip_txt)
    )
    .sort(c.sim_score, descending=True)
    .group_by(c.filepath)
    .head(1)
    .select(class_rate = (c.label == c.text).mean())
)
```

The classifier gets 91.6% of the photographs right, without any training on our
data.

9. Take the code from the previous question, but instead of the last `.select`,
group by `label` and compute the `class_rate` for each breed. Sort from the lowest
to the highest rate.

```{python}
(
    woof
    .join(breed_embed, how="cross")
    .with_columns(
        sim_score = dot_product(c.siglip, c.siglip_txt)
    )
    .sort(c.sim_score, descending=True)
    .group_by(c.filepath)
    .head(1)
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(class_rate = (c.label == c.text).mean())
    .sort(c.class_rate)
)
```

The hardest breeds are the beagle (79%), the English foxhound (82%), and the
Australian terrier (85%). These are the same breeds that looked alike in question 2,
and the two hounds shared a cluster in question 5.
